about: Engineering Practice 1 (AERO40004) is a 10-ECTS core module in Year 1 of Imperial's MEng Aeronautical Engineering, running from the autumn to the summer term. It is practical and small-group based. The module summary lists technical drawing, engineering ethics, manufacturing (including building a wind turbine) and technical communication through lab reports and presentations. It has no fixed lecture syllabus, so this is a guide pack: it explains each strand and gives the standard facts and calculations you will need. We could not load the department's full descriptor, so we do not state assessment weights; check the module page and your assignment briefs.

notes.h: Technical drawing: what you need to be able to do
notes.body:
Engineering Practice 1 is a hands-on module, so drawing is a skill you practise rather than a syllabus you memorise. A few conventions come up again and again, and getting them wrong makes a drawing unusable.

Orthographic projection
- Each view looks straight at one face of the part, so lengths and shapes can be measured directly.
- First-angle projection (usual in the UK and Europe): the plan (view from above) goes below the front view, and the view from the left goes on the right.
- Third-angle projection (usual in North America): the plan goes above the front view, and the view from the left goes on the left.
- Every drawing must show the projection symbol, a truncated cone in side and end view. Don't memorise the symbol as 'circles on the left/right' (diagrams vary in which end of the cone they draw large); read it as a tiny drawing: in first angle the end view is drawn on the opposite side from the end it looks at, in third angle on the same side. Check the version in your course notes.

Lines and views (BS 8888 / ISO 128)
- Continuous wide lines for visible edges.
- Dashed narrow lines for hidden edges.
- Long-dash dotted narrow lines for centre lines.
- Continuous narrow lines for dimensions and hatching.
- Section views (hatched at 45°) show internal features more clearly than hidden lines.

Dimensioning
- Dimension each feature once, in millimetres, from functional datums: the faces or axes that locate the part.
- Avoid long chains of dimensions, because their tolerances add up.
- Never dimension to a hidden line.

Tolerancing
Every dimension needs limits, because nothing can be made exactly to size.
- A general tolerance note, for example a reference to ISO 2768-m (±0.2 mm for sizes over 6 mm and up to 30 mm), covers dimensions without their own tolerance.
- Where parts must fit together, use the ISO 286 limits and fits system on a hole basis.
- Example: a Ø25 H7 hole is 25.000–25.021 mm. With a g6 shaft (24.980–24.993 mm), the clearance is 0.007–0.041 mm, a sliding fit. A p6 shaft (25.022–25.035 mm) gives an interference of 0.001–0.035 mm, which needs pressing in.
- When several parts stack up, worst-case tolerance is the sum of the individual tolerances. The statistical (root-sum-square) estimate is √(Σt²).

How to prepare
- Practise sketching simple brackets in both projections from a 3D view, and the reverse.
- Check your drawings against a list: projection symbol, title block (title, scale, units, material, author, date), centre lines on every hole, no duplicated dimensions, sensible tolerances.
- Think about how the part will be made. A tolerance tighter than the workshop process can hold costs time and is pointless if the function does not need it.

Exam tips: in any written check, give actual numbers for limits and fits rather than just letters.

Professional engineers are trusted with public safety. The UK's framework for ethical conduct is the Statement of Ethical Principles, published jointly by the Engineering Council and the Royal Academy of Engineering. The latest version was published in February 2026. It sets out five principles:
- Honesty and integrity
- Responsibility to society
- Accuracy and rigour
- Leadership and communication
- Responsibility for the future of technology, society, and the environment. This principle is new in the 2026 version.

Professional bodies such as the Royal Aeronautical Society add their own codes of conduct. Registered engineers (EngTech, IEng, CEng) are expected to follow them. The competence standard for registration is UK-SPEC.

What the principles mean in practice
- Do not overstate your results, hide data that does not fit, or claim others' work as your own. In coursework, this means honest lab data and correct referencing.
- Work within your competence, and say clearly when something is outside it.
- Put the safety of the public ahead of the interests of an employer or client.
- Raise concerns early and in writing. Escalate them if they are ignored. In the UK, the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 gives legal protection to workers who make certain disclosures in the public interest ("whistleblowing").
- Consider sustainability, the environment and the long-term effects of what you build.

Well-known aerospace cases often used in teaching
- Space Shuttle Challenger (1986). Engineers raised concerns about the performance of the solid rocket booster O-ring seals in cold weather, but the launch went ahead and the vehicle broke up shortly after lift-off. The case is studied for how engineering judgement was overridden by managerial pressure, and for how risk was communicated.
- Boeing 737 MAX (Lion Air Flight 610, October 2018; Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, March 2019). Both crashes involved the MCAS flight control function. The case raises questions about design assumptions, single points of failure, pilot training and information, and the relationship between manufacturer and regulator.

When discussing cases, separate what is established by official investigation from opinion, and focus on the decisions engineers faced and the principles at stake.

Professional skills you will use in group practical work
- Teamwork: agree roles, deadlines and how decisions are made, and keep a shared record of who did what.
- Planning: break the task into steps, identify what depends on what, and leave time for things to go wrong, especially in the workshop.
- Health and safety: follow workshop rules, risk-assess activities and report near misses.
- Communication: write clearly for the reader (topic 4).

How to prepare
Read the Statement of Ethical Principles, practise applying the principles to short scenarios (data falsification, cutting corners under time pressure, conflicts of interest), and be ready to justify a decision rather than just name a principle.

notes.h: Manufacturing and the wind turbine build
notes.body:
The module's practical work includes manufacturing, with a small wind turbine as a build task. Groups therefore need basic workshop calculations and enough turbine theory to understand what they are measuring.

Workshop calculations
- Spindle speed for turning, milling or drilling: N = 1000 V/(π D). N is in rpm, V is the recommended cutting speed in m/min and D is the work or tool diameter in mm.
- Example: an 8 mm drill at 25 m/min needs about 995 rpm. A 40 mm bar turned at 120 m/min needs about 955 rpm.
- Milling feed rate: vf = fz × z × N, where fz is the feed per tooth and z the number of teeth.
- Choose the process from the material, the shape, the accuracy needed and the number of parts. Additive manufacturing (for example FDM) is quick for complex one-off shapes such as blades, but its surface finish and dimensional accuracy are limited. Machining gives accurate hubs and shafts. Laser cutting suits flat parts.
- Workshop safety: eye protection, no loose clothing, guards in place, and swarf cleared with a brush, never by hand.

Wind turbine basics
- The power carried by the wind through the rotor disc is P = ½ ρ A V³, with A = π R².
- The rotor extracts a fraction of this, measured by the power coefficient: P = Cp × ½ ρ A V³.
- Because power depends on V³, doubling the wind speed gives eight times the power. Because A = πR², doubling the radius gives four times the power.
- The Betz limit is the maximum Cp an ideal open rotor can achieve: 16/27 ≈ 0.593. Real small turbines are well below this.
- Tip speed ratio: λ = ωR/V, the blade tip speed divided by the wind speed. Cp varies with λ and peaks at an optimum value, so performance is normally plotted as Cp against λ.

Worked example
Take R = 0.3 m, V = 8 m/s and ρ = 1.225 kg/m³.
- A = 0.283 m², so the wind power through the disc is ½ × 1.225 × 0.283 × 8³ = 88.7 W.
- With Cp = 0.3, the turbine produces 26.6 W. The Betz maximum would be 52.5 W.
- At 1500 rpm, ω = 157 rad/s, so λ = 157 × 0.3/8 = 5.9.
- If a test gives a shaft torque of 0.12 N m at 1200 rpm, the shaft power is 0.12 × 125.7 = 15.1 W, so Cp = 15.1/88.7 = 0.17.

Making it work
- Balance the rotor and keep the blades identical: imbalance causes vibration and can make the test unsafe.
- Check the blade pitch angle and the aerofoil orientation before testing.
- Measure the wind speed at the rotor plane, not somewhere else in the tunnel.
- Keep a build log of what was changed and why, so you can explain your results.

How to prepare
Revise P = ½ρAV³Cp, the Betz limit and the tip speed ratio, and practise the spindle speed formula.

Much of the assessment in practical modules depends on how well you communicate what you did. A good report lets a reader repeat your work and judge your conclusions.

Structure of a technical report
- Title and summary (abstract): what was done, the key numbers and the main conclusion, in a few sentences.
- Introduction: the aim and why it matters.
- Theory: only the equations you use, with symbols defined.
- Method and apparatus: enough detail to repeat the experiment. Use past tense and the passive voice or "we", following your department's style.
- Results: tables and figures, each numbered and captioned, with labelled axes and units.
- Discussion: compare with theory, explain the differences, and analyse sources of error.
- Conclusions: answer the aim directly, using numbers.
- References in a consistent style, plus appendices for raw data.

Figures and numbers
- Plot measured data as points (markers), not joined-up lines. Draw theory as a line.
- Give results to a sensible number of significant figures, consistent with their uncertainty, for example 0.17 ± 0.01, not 0.170683.
- Every quantity needs units.

Uncertainty
- Distinguish random errors (scatter, reduced by repeating and averaging) from systematic errors (bias, such as an uncalibrated sensor, which repeating does not remove).
- For independent random uncertainties:
- Sums and differences: add absolute uncertainties in quadrature, so δz = √(δx² + δy²).
- Products and quotients: add relative uncertainties in quadrature. For P = Tω with torque ±2% and speed ±1%, δP/P = √(2² + 1²) = ±2.2%. The worst case would be ±3%.
- Powers: multiply the relative uncertainty by the power. For V³, a ±1% error in V becomes ±3% in V³. This is why wind speed measurement matters so much for turbine Cp.
- Standard error of a mean of n readings: s/√n.

Presentations
- One message per slide, few words, large readable figures.
- Rehearse to time, and share the speaking fairly in group presentations.
- Start with the aim, end with the conclusions, and be ready for questions about your method and uncertainties.

Academic integrity
Reference all sources, including figures you did not make. Make your own contribution clear in group work. Never alter data. The links to the ethics principles in topic 2 are direct.

How to prepare
Before writing, read the marking criteria for each report or presentation (they are given for each assessment). Draft the figures first, then write the text around them.

questions.q: On a first-angle drawing, where is the view looking from the left of the front view placed?
options: To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view
questions.why: In first-angle projection the object sits between the viewer and the plane, so the view seen from the left is projected onto a plane on the right and drawn there. Placing it on the left is the third-angle convention. Above the front view is where third angle puts the plan. Below the front view is where first angle puts the plan, not the side view.

questions.q: A team member suggests deleting two outlying data points from your group's wind tunnel results, with no reason except that they spoil the trend. Which principle in the Statement of Ethical Principles most directly applies?
options: Responsibility for the future of technology, society, and the environment
questions.why: Removing data without a technical justification misrepresents the results, which goes to honesty and integrity. Accuracy and rigour is also relevant, but it is not among these options. Leadership and communication concerns how engineers lead teams and communicate, which is secondary here. Responsibility for the future of technology, society and the environment concerns long-term effects on the world, not the handling of a data set. Responsibility to society is about safeguarding the public, and is not the main issue in a coursework data set.

questions.q: A turbine of radius 0.3 m in an 8 m/s wind (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) has Cp = 0.3. What power does it produce?
questions.why: P = Cp × ½ρπR²V³ = 0.3 × 0.5 × 1.225 × π × 0.09 × 512 = 26.6 W. 106 W uses the 0.6 m diameter as the radius, which makes the area four times too big. 3.3 W uses V² instead of V³. 53.2 W leaves out the factor of one half.

options: The maximum power coefficient of an ideal open rotor, 16/27 ≈ 0.593
The tip speed ratio at which a turbine stalls
The wind speed above which a turbine must shut down
The maximum efficiency of a generator, about 0.95
questions.why: Betz showed that an ideal open rotor can extract at most 16/27 of the wind's power passing through its disc, because the air must keep moving to leave the rotor. Stall depends on blade angle of attack and is not what the Betz limit describes. Shutdown (cut-out) wind speed is a design and safety choice for a particular machine, not a theoretical limit. Generator efficiency is a separate electrical loss.

questions.q: In a wind tunnel test at V = 8 m/s, your group's 0.3 m-radius rotor gives a shaft torque of 0.12 N m at 1200 rpm. Calculate the shaft power, the power coefficient and the tip speed ratio, and comment against the Betz limit (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³).
markScheme: Comment: well below Betz (0.593); losses from blade profile, tip losses, friction; test other λ to find the optimum
questions.modelAnswer: ω = 2π × 1200/60 = 125.7 rad/s, so the shaft power is P = Tω = 0.12 × 125.7 = 15.1 W. The wind power through the disc is ½ × 1.225 × π × 0.3² × 8³ = 88.7 W, so Cp = 15.1/88.7 = 0.17. The tip speed ratio is λ = ωR/V = 125.7 × 0.3/8 = 4.7. A Cp of 0.17 is far below the Betz limit of 0.593, which is normal for a small hand-built rotor. Profile drag on the blades, tip losses, imperfect blade geometry and bearing friction all reduce it. The rotor should be tested over a range of loads, and hence tip speed ratios, to find where Cp peaks.

questions.q: Shaft power is calculated as P = Tω. Torque is known to ±2% and speed to ±1%, and the errors are independent. What is the uncertainty in P?
questions.why: For a product of independent quantities, the relative uncertainties add in quadrature: √(2² + 1²) = 2.24%. ±3% simply adds them, which is the worst case and overstates the likely error for independent errors. ±1.5% is just the average of the two, which has no statistical basis. ±2% keeps only the larger term and ignores the speed uncertainty.
